FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Dinosaur flashcards.

Thirty-three dinosaurs, thirty-three ways to move. Each card names one dinosaur — the famous red hunter, the three-horned friend, the plated one with the swishing tail — and prints one activity under its name: stomp like a T. rex, stretch your neck up high, flap your arms and glide. Each card page carries the card, its action and one way to play it tonight; each dinosaur also gets a full lesson and a printable twin in the library. The deck opens with the six dinosaurs every child asks for first and walks the rest of the prehistoric world from there.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Dino moves day

    Deal five cards face down, turn one over, do its action together, then turn the next. Five minutes later the whole living room has roared, glided and stomped — and nobody noticed it was exercise.

  2. 02

    Big, bigger, biggest

    Line the cards up from smallest to tallest — a five-centimeter Compsognathus to a bus-length Diplodocus. Your child has just built a real size scale without a single worksheet.

  3. 03

    Roar train

    One child picks a card and does its action; everyone else copies and follows behind in a line. When the leader calls another dinosaur, the whole train switches its move.

  4. 04

    Which one is hiding?

    Hold up three cards, name each dinosaur, then turn them face down and slide one away. Which dinosaur is gone? The memory game paleontologists wish they had.

  5. 05

    Plant eater or hunter?

    Sort the deck into two piles by what each dinosaur ate. The toothy ones go left, the leafy ones go right — science sorting, learned with the first sort.

      Tyrannosaurus Rex Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Tyrannosaurus Rex is the most famous dinosaur of all: a giant hunter with a jaw full of banana-sized teeth and arms so small they make everyone laugh. This card turns that giant into a game — stand tall, lift one big foot, and stomp like a T. rex.

      Say it together

      “Tyrannosaurus Rex! The king of the dinosaurs — roar big, lift your giant foot, and STOMP. One stomp, two stomps — the whole floor shakes!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stomp around the room like the biggest dinosaur ever, then shrink: tiptoe like a baby T. rex sneaking up on its dinner. Big feet, little feet, big roar, tiny squeak — the switch is the game.

      Quick parent note

      A real T. rex grew as long as a school bus and its bite was the strongest of any land animal ever found. Its arms were shorter than your arms — and nobody knows exactly why.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tyrannosaurus Rex lesson on the Learning Path.

      Triceratops Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Triceratops wears three horns and a big bony frill like a shield on its head. It munched plants all day and used its horns to say "not today" to anything bossy. The card’s action: put three pretend horns on your face and show them off.

      Say it together

      “Triceratops! Three horns — one, two, three! Put your horns on, swing your head gently, and munch, munch, munch the tall grass.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Point two finger-horns from your forehead and one from your nose, then walk in a slow circle showing them to the whole family. Swap: who can make the proudest triceratops frill with their arms?

      Quick parent note

      Triceratops means "three-horned face." Its frill was bone — a real shield — and its beak could snip a branch like scissors.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Triceratops lesson on the Learning Path.

      Stegosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Stegosaurus carries a row of leaf-shaped plates along its back and four sharp spikes at the end of its tail. It was a plant eater that swished its tail to keep trouble away. The card’s action: pretend to swish your tail — slowly at first, then whoosh.

      Say it together

      “Stegosaurus! Plates up on your back, spikes ready on your tail — swish, swish, SWISH the tail and keep the bossy dinosaurs away!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tuck a scarf or a sock in your waistband as a tail and swish it in big slow arcs. Then freeze like a statue with plates standing tall — can anyone guess which dinosaur you are?

      Quick parent note

      The plates were about as big as car wheels and may have helped the stegosaurus stay cool. Its brain was around the size of a plum — and it did just fine for millions of years.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Stegosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Brachiosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Brachiosaurus is the tall one: front legs longer than its back legs, a neck like a tower crane, and a head that grazed the treetops where no other dinosaur could reach. The card’s action: reach up high like a Brachiosaurus — the tallest stretch in the room wins.

      Say it together

      “Brachiosaurus! The tall one — stretch your neck up, up, UP to the very tallest leaves. Munch, munch — yummy treetop salad!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stretch arms straight up and walk slowly on tiptoe, picking pretend leaves from door frames and lampshades. Then crouch low and pick grass like a little dinosaur — tall stretch, small nibble, tall stretch again.

      Quick parent note

      A brachiosaurus could hold its head four stories high — taller than most houses. It ate hundreds of pounds of leaves every single day.

      Teach it, step by step

      Pterodactyl Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Flyers & swimmers

      The Pterodactyl is the sky-dinosaur everyone points at: wide leathery wings, a long beak and a head crest riding the wind. Technically a flying reptile rather than a dinosaur — a fact young paleontologists love to correct. The card’s action: flap your arms and glide.

      Say it together

      “Pterodactyl! Wings out, flap, flap, flap — and GLIDE! Soar over the mountains, dip down low, and scoop a fish right out of the water!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Flap five times, then hold still and glide across the rug. Land on a "cliff" (the couch arm), then take off again. Score one point per glide that ends softly.

      Quick parent note

      Pterodactyl wings were made of skin stretched over long finger bones — the fourth finger was as long as the whole arm. Some pterosaurs were as tall as giraffes when standing.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pterodactyl lesson on the Learning Path.

      Velociraptor Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Velociraptor is the quick one: small, fast and light, sprinting on two legs with one big claw raised on each foot. The card’s action: take three quick dino steps — then freeze and look around like a clever hunter.

      Say it together

      “Velociraptor! Quick, quick, quick — three fast dino steps, then FREEZE. Where did everybody go? A raptor has fast feet and fast eyes!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Run three quick steps, freeze, look left and right, then three more. Play it as a race across the room — first one to the far wall with three freezes on the way is the champion raptor.

      Quick parent note

      A real velociraptor was about the size of a turkey and covered in feathers — the movie monsters got the size wrong. Its foot claw could fold back like a pocketknife.

      Teach it, step by step

      Allosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Allosaurus was the big hunter long before the T. rex: sharp teeth, a ridged brow and a mouth that opened unbelievably wide. The card’s action: take two giant dino roars — one for each side of the room.

      Say it together

      “Allosaurus! A big hunter with a bigger mouth — take a deep breath and ROAR one giant roar... and now the biggest roar of all. ROOOAR!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Roar once facing the window, once facing the door. Then whisper both roars — baby allosaurus size. Loud, louder, tiny: the volume switch is what makes roaring a real game.

      Quick parent note

      Allosaurus means "different lizard." Its jaw could swing open extra wide, and it is one of the most common big dinosaurs ever dug up.

      Ankylosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Ankylosaurus is the armored tank of the dinosaur world: a studded back like a knight’s shield and a heavy round club at the end of its tail. The card’s action: pretend to swing your club tail — slow and heavy, never fast.

      Say it together

      “Ankylosaurus! Armor on your back, club on your tail — swing it sloooowly around... thud! Nobody bothers an ankylosaurus twice!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold a soft cushion as your club and swing it in a slow semicircle around your feet. Then sit down, tuck in like the armored ball the card shows, and see who can guess what you are.

      Quick parent note

      The tail club was made of two lumps of bone fused together — a real hammer. An ankylosaurus weighed as much as a car and its armor was up to a finger thick.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Ankylosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Archaeopteryx Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Flyers & swimmers

      The Archaeopteryx is the famous half-way dinosaur: feathers like a bird, teeth like a dinosaur, wings that could flutter but probably preferred gliding. The card’s action: stretch your wings — out wide, up high, one then the other.

      Say it together

      “Archaeopteryx! Half dinosaur, half bird — stretch your feathered wings out wiiide... flap a little... glide a little. The very first flying cousin!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stretch both arms out like wings, then bow one wing at a time to each side. Flap three small flutters, then glide to a perch. Feathers on your head add instant archaeopteryx power.

      Quick parent note

      The first archaeopteryx fossil was found in Germany in 1861 with its feathers printed in stone. Birds are its living grandchildren — chickens included.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Archaeopteryx lesson on the Learning Path.

      Baryonyx Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Baryonyx is the fisher dinosaur: a long narrow snout like a crocodile, a big claw on one thumb, and a real love of lunch from the river. The card’s action: pretend to catch a fish — paw in the water, wait, then scoop.

      Say it together

      “Baryonyx! The fish catcher — dip your claw in the river, wait... wait... SWOOSH! A fish for lunch! Snap, munch, yummy!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stand on one leg as the riverbank, dip one hand low, hold perfectly still for three seconds, then scoop the fish up and gobble it. Alternating hands keeps the fishing trip going all afternoon.

      Quick parent note

      Scientists found fish scales and a lemon-sized claw inside a baryonyx’s belly — proof of its fish supper. Its teeth numbered almost a hundred.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Baryonyx lesson on the Learning Path.

      Carnotaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Carnotaurus is the bull of the dinosaurs: two horns above its eyes, a snub face and arms so tiny they are almost a joke. The card’s action: make tiny horn poses — horns forward, head low, best fierce face.

      Say it together

      “Carnotaurus! The bull-headed hunter — put your two horns on, lower your head, and POSE. Fierce face... prouder face... the fiercest face of all!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Point two fingers above your eyebrows, lower your head and strike three poses: fierce, proud, silly. Everyone else copies the pose — the silliest pose gets the biggest roar.

      Quick parent note

      Carnotaurus means "meat-eating bull." Its arms were smaller than a T. rex’s — some scientists think they were barely any use at all.

      Teach it, step by step

      Centrosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Centrosaurus is a horned plant eater with a big frill edged in little spikes and one strong horn on its nose. It traveled in giant herds — hundreds of frills moving together across the plain. The card’s action: make a gentle horn pose.

      Say it together

      “Centrosaurus! One strong horn on your nose, a big frill behind your head — make a gentle horn pose and nod hello to the whole herd.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Touch your nose-horn forward, hold your arm-frill up and walk a slow herd circle with everyone else posing too. Gentle is the rule: the pose is for saying hello, not for bumping.

      Quick parent note

      Centrosaurus herds may have numbered in the thousands — a whole town of horned plant eaters. Its frill spikes made the herd look like a walking garden of thorns.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Centrosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Ceratosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Ceratosaurus is the horn-nosed hunter: a small horn on its snout, ridges along its back and a long tail for balance while it ran. The card’s action: make a tiny horn pose — small horn, big attitude.

      Say it together

      “Ceratosaurus! A hunter with a tiny horn on its nose — tap your nose, make your horn, and pose with your proudest hunter face.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tap the tip of your nose for the horn, strike a pose, then stomp three steps and pose again. The game is posing in new places: doorway pose, couch pose, window pose.

      Quick parent note

      Ceratosaurus had bony ridges above each eye as well as its nose horn — a face full of decorations. It swam better than most big hunters, judging by its strong tail.

      Teach it, step by step

      Compsognathus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Compsognathus is the chicken-sized hunter: slim, quick and light as a loaf of bread. Where big dinosaurs thunder, this one tiptoes. The card’s action: take five tiny dino steps — count them out loud, one to five.

      Say it together

      “Compsognathus! The littlest hunter — tiny steps now: one, two, three, four, five! Small feet, quick eyes, and off you scoot!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take five tiptoe steps, freeze, then five more. Try five tiny steps backward, five sideways, five in a circle. Little dinosaurs can go anywhere — quietly.

      Quick parent note

      A full-grown compsognathus was about the size of a chicken and could fit on a dinner plate. One fossil was found with a whole lizard inside its stomach.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Compsognathus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Corythosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Corythosaurus wears a rounded crest swept back from its head like a half-moon — and that hollow crest may have worked like a trumpet. The card’s action: pretend to make a trumpet call — deep breath, then one long note.

      Say it together

      “Corythosaurus! A trumpet on its head — take a deep breath and call the herd: TOOOTO! Long and low, loud and proud!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hands cupped around your mouth as the crest, make one long trumpet note, then three short ones. The herd answers: everyone else echoes the call back — long, short, short.

      Quick parent note

      The crest’s hollow tubes connected to its nose, so a corythosaurus may have honked like a brass band. Fossils show it could also puff its crest bigger.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Corythosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Deinonychus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Deinonychus is the famous sickle-claw hunter: striped, striped-fast, with a huge curved claw on each foot held up like a switchblade. The card’s action: take quick dino steps — fast feet, then a springy jump and freeze.

      Say it together

      “Deinonychus! Quick feet, big claw — run-run-run, JUMP, and freeze with your claws up! The fastest hunter in the forest is you!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take six quick steps, jump high with both claw-hands up, and freeze like a statue. Do it across the whole room — the jump-freeze at the end is the part everyone repeats.

      Quick parent note

      Deinonychus means "terrible claw," and its foot claw was curved like a banana. It probably hunted in packs, and it is the dinosaur that made scientists rethink what dinosaurs really were.

      Teach it, step by step

      Diplodocus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Diplodocus is the longest of the long: neck forward, whip tail back, a body like a bridge between them. It swept its neck through treetops like a comb. The card’s action: stretch your neck up high — then let your tail swing long behind.

      Say it together

      “Diplodocus! Long neck one way, long tail the other — stretch up high and munch the leaves... now swish that long tail behind you!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stand tall, reach one arm up as the neck and let the other arm trail as the tail, then walk a slow loop around the room. Swap ends: now the tail arm leads and the neck arm follows.

      Quick parent note

      A diplodocus could measure as long as two cars parked end to end — most of it neck and tail. The tail worked like a whip, and some scientists think it could crack it like one too.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Diplodocus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Euoplocephalus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Euoplocephalus is the armored cousin of the ankylosaurus: a wide studded back, armor even on its eyelids, and a low club tail. Its best trick is tucking everything safe under the armor. The card’s action: pretend to curl into a ball.

      Say it together

      “Euoplocephalus! Armor all over — curl in small, tuck your head, hide under your shields. Nobody can find you now!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Curl up small on the floor with your arms tucked in — count to five all tucked — then unfold into a giant armored dinosaur and stomp twice. Curl, count, unfold: the safest game in the deck.

      Quick parent note

      Even the euoplocephalus’s eyelids had sliding bones like little shutters. Its club tail could swing low and hard enough to dent a real attacker.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Euoplocephalus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Giganotosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Giganotosaurus may have been even longer than the T. rex — a giant southern-hemisphere hunter with a huge head and an enormous grin. The card’s action: take three giant steps, the longest steps your legs can make.

      Say it together

      “Giganotosaurus! Even bigger than a T. rex — three GIANT steps: one... two... three! Can your giant steps cross the whole room?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take three giant steps from one wall and see where you land, then three more. Measure: how many giant steps does the hallway take? A baby giga takes baby steps — tiny ones still count.

      Quick parent note

      Giganotosaurus means "giant southern lizard." Its teeth were as long as your hand, and one fossil was found near the bones of the biggest plant eater ever discovered.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Giganotosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Hadrosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Hadrosaurus is the classic duck-bill: a wide flat beak for cropping plants and strong back legs that could run or wade. The card’s action: pretend to nibble leaves — small bites, happy chewing.

      Say it together

      “Hadrosaurus! A duck bill for a mouth — nibble, nibble, nibble the leaves. Small bites, chomp chomp — a plant eater is always polite at lunch!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pick pretend leaves at three heights — low grass, bush height, up on tiptoe — and nibble each one with different sounds. Finish with one big happy chomp and a satisfied dinosaur sigh.

      Quick parent note

      Hadrosaurus was the first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton ever dug up in North America, back in 1858. Duck bills chewed side to side, like a horse.

      Iguanodon Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Iguanodon is one of the first dinosaurs ever named: a plant eater that walked on two legs or four, with a sharp thumb spike for keeping its distance. The card’s action: pretend to munch leaves — reach, strip the branch, munch.

      Say it together

      “Iguanodon! Reach out with your hand, grab the branch, and MUNCH munch munch. Thumbs up, spike ready — nobody pushes an iguanodon around!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Reach one arm out, strip pretend leaves off with your other hand, and munch with big exaggerated chews. Give a thumbs-up spike at the end — the iguanodon signature.

      Quick parent note

      Iguanodon’s thumb spike confused scientists for years — early guesses put it on the nose. It could switch from four legs to two when it needed speed.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Iguanodon lesson on the Learning Path.

      Maiasaura Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Maiasaura is the good-mother dinosaur: fossils show it fed and looked after its babies in crowded nesting colonies. The card’s action: gently care for a baby dino — wrap, feed, and pat-pat-pat.

      Say it together

      “Maiasaura! The mummy dinosaur — cuddle your baby dino, feed it leaves, and pat, pat, pat it to sleep. A good mother makes a warm nest!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Cuddle a stuffed animal as the baby, pretend-feed it leaves, tuck it into a cushion nest and pat its head five times. Then swap: your child is the baby being cared for — giggles guaranteed.

      Quick parent note

      Maiasaura means "good mother lizard." Its nests held about thirty eggs, and babies stayed in the nest while parents brought food — the first proof that some dinosaurs were caring parents.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Maiasaura lesson on the Learning Path.

      Microraptor Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Flyers & swimmers

      The Microraptor is the four-winged wonder: wings on its arms AND its legs, glossy feathers, and a glide between trees that must have looked like magic. The card’s action: flap your little wings — quick small flaps, not big ones.

      Say it together

      “Microraptor! Four little wings — flap, flap, flap them fast! Small wings, shiny feathers, and off it glides between the trees!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Flap hands and feet together for three seconds — four wings working — then hold a glide pose with arms and legs spread. Jump from cushion to cushion as tree to tree.

      Quick parent note

      Microraptor fossils preserved the color of its feathers: shiny black with a blue-green sheen, like a starling. It was barely bigger than a pigeon.

      Teach it, step by step

      Mosasaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Flyers & swimmers

      The Mosasaurus is the sea monster of the deck: a giant swimming reptile with long jaws, four flippers and a shark-style tail. It was not a dinosaur — it ruled the waves while dinosaurs ruled the land. The card’s action: make a big swimming motion.

      Say it together

      “Mosasaurus! The king of the ancient sea — arms out, swim, swim, swim... dive deep, then SNAP those long jaws at a fishy lunch!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Lie on your tummy and do one big swimming stroke, arms sweeping wide, then pop up for a jaw-snap. Glide around the room like the sea is everywhere — the floor counts as ocean.

      Quick parent note

      A mosasaurus could grow longer than a bus and ate fish, sharks and even other mosasaurs. It breathed air like a whale, so it surfaced for breath between hunts.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Mosasaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Ouranosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Ouranosaurus carries a tall rounded sail along its back, like a sail catching the desert sun. The card’s action: make a tall back sail — arch your back and show how big your sail can be.

      Say it together

      “Ouranosaurus! A sail on its back — arch up tall and make your sail BIGGER... and bigger! Look at that sail catching the sunshine!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Arch your back and stretch your arms behind as the sail, growing taller and taller until the sail is enormous — then flop flat like a tired dinosaur and start again.

      Quick parent note

      The sail may have worked like a built-in heater and cooler, warming in the morning sun and dumping heat in the shade. Its name means "brave lizard."

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Ouranosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Oviraptor Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Oviraptor got an unfair name — "egg thief" — because it was found near eggs. Scientists later learned it was guarding its OWN nest, wings spread over its babies. The card’s action: pretend to protect an egg.

      Say it together

      “Oviraptor! The nest keeper — curl your arms around your egg and keep it safe. Gentle wings over the egg... shhh, the baby is sleeping!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Cup your hands as the egg, then wrap both arms around it and stand guard, walking in slow circles around the nest. Someone else tries a gentle "steal" — the guardian shields without letting go.

      Quick parent note

      One famous oviraptor fossil was found sitting on its nest just like a brooding bird, with eggs still underneath. Its strong beak could crack seeds and shellfish — maybe eggs too, but mostly its own snacks.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Oviraptor lesson on the Learning Path.

      Pachycephalosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Pachycephalosaurus has the strangest head in the deck: a thick bone dome like a helmet, ten fingers thick. Two of them may have bumped heads gently to decide who was boss. The card’s action: pretend to bump gently.

      Say it together

      “Pachycephalosaurus! A helmet made of bone — pat your round head, stand tall, and bump very gently: boop! Gentle bumps only — we are friendly dinosaurs!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stand on one leg, pat your dome head twice, then lean in for a gentle shoulder bump with a partner — boop! The softest bump wins the boss crown.

      Quick parent note

      The dome was solid bone up to ten inches thick. Its bumps were probably gentle shoves rather than head-on crashes — dinosaur manners were better than the movies say.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pachycephalosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Parasaurolophus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Parasaurolophus is the one with the famous tube crest sweeping back from its head — a built-in horn that could boom across the whole valley. The card’s action: pretend to make a dino call.

      Say it together

      “Parasaurolophus! A horn growing from its head — breathe in deep and call: HOOOOONK! Can the herd hear you from far, far away?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Rest one forearm along the back of your head as the crest, breathe in and make one long deep honk. The herd answers with its own honks — first loud, then whisper-honks for the evening.

      Quick parent note

      Scientists built a model of the crest’s tubes and played its sound — a deep foghorn honk you can hear online. The crest on a grown male was nearly as long as the dinosaur’s skull.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Parasaurolophus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Plateosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Plateosaurus is one of the oldest plant eaters on the cards: a long-necked, long-tailed early giant that stood up on its hind legs to reach the high branches. The card’s action: reach for the tallest leaves.

      Say it together

      “Plateosaurus! One of the very first long necks — stand up tall, reach out your arm, and pick the very tallest leaves. Higher... higher... you got one!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pick three pretend leaves at three heights: knee, shoulder and tiptoe-reach. Munch each one twice, then bend down and graze like a four-legged dinosaur — the same animal, two feeding styles.

      Quick parent note

      Plateosaurus herds walked Europe about 210 million years ago — long before T. rex was even a twinkle. It could rear up on two legs or amble on four.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Plateosaurus lesson on the Learning Path.

      Quetzalcoatlus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Flyers & swimmers

      The Quetzalcoatlus is the biggest flyer that ever lived — a pterosaur with a wingspan as wide as a small plane, stalking on folded wings between take-offs. The card’s action: flap and glide like a giant flyer.

      Say it together

      “Quetzalcoatlus! The giant of the sky — big slow flaps, then a loooong glide. Such a big flyer does not need to hurry!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take three enormous slow flaps, then glide with arms spread for five whole seconds. Land tall on straight legs — a giant pterosaur walks proudly, then takes off again.

      Quick parent note

      Quetzalcoatlus is named after a feathered serpent god. Standing on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe, and its wings stretched about ten meters tip to tip.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Spinosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Hunters & chasers

      The Spinosaurus is the sail-backed giant: a crocodile snout, a huge back sail and a real love of rivers and fish. It may have been the longest meat-eating dinosaur of all. The card’s action: make a big sail with your arms.

      Say it together

      “Spinosaurus! A sail as big as a door on its back — lift your arms up high and make YOUR big sail. Now snap that long snout at a fish!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sweep both arms up behind your head into one big sail shape, hold it tall, then flop into a swim and snap your snout hands three times. Sail, swim, snap — the spinosaurus routine.

      Quick parent note

      The spines holding up the sail were taller than your whole arm. Spinosaurus ate fish mostly, and its flat feet and paddle tail made it a strong swimmer.

      Teach it, step by step

      Styracosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Styracosaurus is the spiky-frilled showpiece: a crown of long spikes ringing its frill and one big horn on its nose. The card’s action: make a brave horn pose — spikes out, head up, courage on.

      Say it together

      “Styracosaurus! A crown of spikes around your frill — spread your spike-arms, lift your head, and make the bravest horn pose of all!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fan your fingers out around your head as the spikes, take one big brave step forward and hold the pose for three seconds. Then shuffle sideways in a herd line, poses up, no bumping.

      Quick parent note

      The frill spikes were nearly as long as your arm — six of them crowning the frill. It weighed about as much as a small car and defended itself with that nose horn.

      Therizinosaurus Flashcard for Dinosaurs

      Ages 3+Horned, plated & plant eaters

      The Therizinosaurus is the claw champion: a tall, round-bellied plant eater with claws longer than your whole arm — the longest claws of any animal ever found. The card’s action: show your long claws.

      Say it together

      “Therizinosaurus! The longest claws in the world — stretch your arms out and show those giant claws... so long! So wavy! And still a gentle leaf eater!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Extend both arms wide, curl your fingers into long pretend claws and wave them slowly like feather dusters. Then hook an invisible high branch and pull down a leafy breakfast.

      Quick parent note

      Each claw measured about half a meter — a meter with the finger. Despite the monster claws, therizinosaurus ate plants and probably used its hooks to pull branches down for dinner.
